This British Conservative served as Leader of the House of Commons from 2022 to 2024, ran for party leadership against Liz Truss, and later lost her Portsmouth North seat in 2024 — who is she?
In 1996, a gunman killed 35 people at a historic Tasmanian tourist site, leading to sweeping changes in Australia's gun laws — what is this tragedy called?
Port Arthur massacre: 1996 mass shooting in Tasmania, Australia.
Serving as Ecuador's president from 2007 to 2017, this democratic socialist economist has lived in Belgium since leaving office — who is he?
Rafael Correa: President of Ecuador from 2007 to 2017. Correa won the presidency in the 2006 general election on a platform criticizing the established political elites.
Designated Crown Prince during his father's 1967 coronation, this dissident has lived in exile in the US since the 1979 revolution that abolished the monarchy his family once ruled — who is he?
Reza Pahlavi: Former Crown Prince of Iran (born 1960)
Valedictorian of Plains High School in Georgia, this American first lady became a lifelong champion of mental health and women's rights — who was she?
Rosalynn Carter: First Lady of the United States from 1977 to 1981.
A Harvard graduate and second cousin to a future U.S. president, this Boston revolutionary founded the Sons of Liberty and signed the Declaration of Independence — who was he?
Samuel Adams: Founding Father of the United States (1722–1803)
Rising through the ranks despite the Great Purge of the 1930s, this Soviet officer became a Marshal of the Soviet Union and led the Ukrainian Front during the 1939 invasion of Poland — who is he?

As part of the Battle of the Bulge, this December 1944 clash saw the 101st Airborne help defend a vital Belgian crossroads town where seven main roads converged, blocking the German drive toward Antwerp — which engagement is this?

Siege of Bastogne: American/German engagement December 1944. Until 23 December, the weather prevented Allied aircraft from attempting to resupply Bastogne or from performing ground attack missions against German forces.

On 26 September 1983, this Soviet duty officer judged his early-warning system's report of incoming U.S. missiles to be a false alarm — disobeying protocol and likely averting nuclear war. Who was he?
Stanislav Petrov: Soviet Air Defence Forces officer (1939–2017)
A military engineer who is a national hero in Poland, Lithuania, Belarus AND the United States, he fought for the American Revolution before leading an uprising in 1794 — who was he?

Beginning in 73 BCE with about 70 gladiators escaping a school in Capua, this slave revolt swelled to 120,000 people and became the only such uprising to directly threaten the Roman heartland — what was it called?
Third Servile War: 73–71 BCE Roman slave rebellion.
This branch of Marxism-Leninism is named for the Russian revolutionary who developed it alongside the Left Opposition and the Fourth International — what's it called?
Trotskyism: Variety of Marxism developed by Leon Trotsky.
The last man standing in the Year of the Four Emperors, this Roman founded the Flavian dynasty and was the first emperor to rise from an equestrian family. Who was he?
Vespasian: Roman emperor from AD 69 to 79.
Sometimes anachronistically called Elizabeth, this woman was empress consort to China's last emperor before later becoming empress consort of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo — who was she?
Wanrong: Empress of Manchukuo from 1934 to 1945 (1906–1946)
Alongside Andrew Moray, this Scottish knight won the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297 before being captured and executed for treason in 1305 — who is he?
William Wallace: Scottish knight (1270–1305). Along with Andrew Moray, Wallace defeated an English army at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in September 1297.
October 1973: the holiest day of the Jewish calendar collided with the 10th day of Ramadan when Arab forces launched a surprise attack on Israel. What war broke out?
Yom Kippur War: 1973 war between Israel and Arab states.
Which of these people was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four appeared earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (published 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Wernher von Braun is a physicist. As a young man, von Braun worked in Nazi Germany's rocket development program.
Which one below is best known as a chemist?
Willard Libby is a chemist. For his contributions to the team that developed this process, Libby was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960.
What is the atomic number of Oxygen?
Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
In what year was Frank Oppenheimer born?
Frank Oppenheimer: The younger brother of renowned physicist J.
In what year was Omar Khayyam born?
Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
In what year was Marie Curie born?
Marie Curie: Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
In what year did António de Oliveira Salazar die?
António de Oliveira Salazar: The regime he created lasted until 1974, making it one of the longest-lived authoritarian dictatorships in modern Europe.
In what year did Josef Mengele die?
Josef Mengele: Before the war, Mengele received doctorates in anthropology and medicine, and he began a career as a researcher.
In what year was HIV discovered?
HIV: Without treatment, the average survival time after infection with HIV is estimated to be 9 to 11 years, depending on the HIV subtype.
In what year was Platinum discovered?
Platinum is a chemical element; it has symbol Pt and atomic number 78.
Rituximab: Pfizer. It is given by slow intravenous infusion.
Which country is Grumman F-14 Tomcat from?

Grumman F-14 Tomcat: United States. The Grumman F-14 Tomcat is an American carrier-capable supersonic, twin-engine, tandem two-seat, twin-tail, all-weather-capable variable-sweep wing fighter aircraft.
Who is credited with discovering Thorium?
Thorium: Jöns Jacob Berzelius. Thorium is a chemical element; it has symbol Th and atomic number 90.
Who is credited with discovering Cauchy–Schwarz inequality?
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: Viktor Bunyakovsky. It is considered one of the most important and widely used inequalities in mathematics.
Who is credited with discovering Phosphorus?
Phosphorus: Hennig Brand. Phosphorus is a chemical element; it has symbol P and atomic number 15.

This alternative-medicine practice, a component of traditional Chinese medicine, involves inserting thin needles into the body, though its underlying theories are considered pseudoscientific by mainstream science — what's the practice called?
Acupuncture is a form of alternative medicine and a component of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in which thin needles are inserted into the body.
This large, muscular mastiff-type dog breed descends from ancestors brought to the British North American colonies, where they worked on small farms and ranches — what's the breed?
American Bulldog is a large, muscular breed of mastiff-type dog.
Found only on male deer, except reindeer, this branching structure of bone and cartilage falls off and regrows from scratch each year — what is it?
Antler are extensions of an animal's skull found in members of the Cervidae (deer) family.

This lung condition — the partial collapse of alveoli that reduces gas exchange, usually in just one lung — is a very common finding on chest X-rays, though it's technically distinct from a fluid-filled lung or a full pneumothorax — what is it?
Atelectasis is the partial collapse or closure of a lung resulting in reduced or absent gas exchange, more specifically the collapse of alveoli.
This steel-gray, lightweight metal with atomic number 4 is found in gemstones like aquamarine and emerald, but within the cores of stars it gets destroyed as fast as it forms — what element is it?
Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
Native to South American tropical forests, this thorny ornamental vine, bush, or tree produces large colorful bracts surrounding three small waxy flowers — what is this plant genus?
Bougainvillea (US also BOH-) is a genus of thorny ornamental vines, bushes, and trees belonging to the family Nyctaginaceae.

First synthesized in 1950 by bombarding curium with helium-4 ions, this synthetic actinide element carries atomic number 98, symbol Cf, and the second-highest atomic mass of any element — which element?
Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.

Appearing in early childhood with symptoms like poor coordination and stiff or weak muscles, this group of movement disorders does not worsen over time even though symptoms become more noticeable in a child's first years — which condition?
Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of movement disorders that appear in early childhood.
In 2023, she became the first woman ever to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on her own, honored for her research on women in the labor market — who is this Harvard economist?
Claudia Goldin (born May 14, 1946) is an American economic historian and labor economist.
This fungal plant disease disfigures maize with galls, yet in Mexican cuisine the infected kernels are prized as huitlacoche, a filling for quesadillas and soups — which disease?
Corn smut is a plant disease caused by the pathogenic fungus Mycosarcoma maydis, synonym Ustilago maydis.
Born at the Point McLeay Mission in 1872, this preacher and inventor who registered 10 patents is widely credited as the first Aboriginal Australian published author — who is he?
David Unaipon was an Aboriginal Australian preacher, inventor, and writer who has been widely credited as the first Aboriginal published author.
This scarab superfamily insect is famous for rolling balls of animal droppings, a behavior the Ancient Egyptians linked to the god Khepri — which creature is it?
Dung beetle are beetles that feed on feces.
This discipline systematically applies natural science and mathematics to design solutions like bridges, pacemakers, and spacecraft under real-world constraints. What field is it?
Engineering is the practice of systematically applying natural science and mathematics to design and improve systems, devices, or processes that solve problems under constraints.

This suborder of meat-eating mammals groups together the 'cat-like' carnivorans — cats, hyenas, mongooses, and viverrids — in contrast to their 'dog-like' counterparts in the other major suborder. What suborder is this?
Feliformia is a suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of "cat-like" carnivorans, including cats, hyenas, mongooses, viverrids, and related taxa.
This Austrian-school economist shared the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Gunnar Myrdal for work on how prices communicate information — who is he?
Friedrich Hayek (8 May 1899 - 23 March 1992) was an Austrian economist and philosopher.
The simplest stable amino acid, with just a single hydrogen for a side chain, it's the only common one that isn't chiral and makes up about 35% of collagen — what is it?
Glycine (symbol Gly or G) is an organic compound with the formula C2H5NO2, and is the simplest stable amino acid, distinguished by having a single hydrogen atom as its side chain.

In 1896 this English physician dosed himself with mescaline and wrote one of the first public reports of the trip; he also co-wrote English's first medical textbook on homosexuality and coined the term 'narcissism' — who was he?
Havelock Ellis (2 February 1859 - 8 July 1939) was an English physician, eugenicist, writer, progressive intellectual and social reformer who studied human sexuality.
Running from the shoulder to the elbow, this arm bone connects the scapula to the radius and ulna, with a rounded head and neck at one end and two epicondyles at the other — name this bone?
Humerus (pl.: humeri) is a long bone in the arm that runs from the shoulder to the elbow.
Denoted by the symbol ∞, this concept of the boundless and endless has been debated by philosophers since ancient Greece and by mathematicians since the 17th century — what is it?
Infinity is something which is boundless, limitless, or endless.
This American businessman and chemist owned the Los Angeles Lakers through their 'Showtime' era of the 1980s, winning 10 league championships as majority owner. Who is he?
Jerry Buss (January 27, 1933 - February 18, 2013) was an American businessman, investor, chemist, and philanthropist.
Found from Africa to the Americas, this family of 118 bird species has big heads and sharp bills, and though most picture them by rivers, many actually live deep in forests — what are they?
Kingfisher are a family, the Alcedinidae, of small to medium-sized, brightly coloured birds in the order Coraciiformes.

This group of blood cancers typically begins in the bone marrow and produces abnormal blood cells called blasts. Symptoms include bleeding, bruising, bone pain, and fever due to a lack of normal blood cells — what is this disease?
Leukemia (also spelled leukaemia) is a group of blood cancers that usually begin in the bone marrow and produce high numbers of abnormal blood cells.

With only six species left today, spread across Africa, South America, and Australia, this ancient group's fossil record stretches back over 410 million years to the Early Devonian — what group is it?
Lungfish are freshwater vertebrates belonging to the class Dipnoi.

In 1895 this American psychologist completed every requirement for a Harvard Ph.D., only to be refused the degree because of her gender — yet she still invented the paired-associate learning technique. Who was she?
Mary Whiton Calkins (30 March 1863 - 26 February 1930) was an American philosopher and psychologist, whose work informed theory and research of memory, dreams and the self.
Built primarily from stainless steel, this Soviet supersonic interceptor could exceed Mach 3.2, but doing so risked wrecking its own engines. What aircraft is it?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25 (NATO reporting name: Foxbat) is a supersonic interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft that is among the fastest military aircraft to enter service.
This genus of bacteria lacks a cell wall entirely, making it naturally immune to antibiotics like penicillin that target cell-wall synthesis — name this genus?
Mycoplasma is a genus of bacteria that, like the other members of the class Mollicutes, lack a cell wall (peptidoglycan) around their cell membrane.

Made from unleavened dough rolled flat and then cut, stretched, or extruded into long strips, this staple food appears across cultures — in Italian cuisine, it goes by an entirely different name. What is it, generically?
Noodle are a type of food typically made from unleavened dough which is rolled flat and cut, stretched, or extruded into long strips or strings.
Dubbed the father of nuclear chemistry, he studied under Ernest Rutherford before helping identify the radioactive elements radium, thorium, and protactinium — who is he?
Otto Hahn (8 March 1879 - 28 July 1968) was a German chemist who was a pioneer in the field of radiochemistry.
Recognized by a long beak and an enormous throat pouch used to drain water from scooped-up prey before swallowing, these large water birds come in eight living species worldwide — which birds?
Pelican (genus Pelecanus) are a genus of large water birds that make up the family Pelecanidae.

A perennial legume native to the Eastern Hemisphere, this crop is a staple across the Indian Subcontinent, Africa and the Caribbean despite a name that sounds more like a bird than a bean. What is it?
Pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) is a perennial legume from the family Fabaceae native to the Eastern Hemisphere.
Domesticated roughly 8,000 years ago in Southeast Asia, chickens are the most common example of this category of farmed birds — what's the term?
Poultry are domesticated birds kept by humans for the purpose of harvesting animal products such as meat, eggs or feathers.
Named partly for the Aztec feathered serpent god and partly for the designer of a tailless aircraft, this genus of giant pterosaur soared over Late Cretaceous North America — what is it?
Quetzalcoatlus is a genus of azhdarchid pterosaur that lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in North America.
Holding a professorship in biology, neurology, and neurosurgery at Stanford, this primatologist is also a research associate with Kenya's National Museums — who is he?
Robert Sapolsky (born April 6, 1957) is an American academic, neuroscientist, and primatologist.
Spanning continents from North America to temperate Asia, this genus covers the majority of the world's common bushy-tailed squirrels — which genus?
Sciurus (or) contains most of the common, bushy-tailed squirrels in North America, Europe, temperate Asia, Central America and South America.
Long, thin and transparent, this hydrozoan drifts through the ocean as a colony of specialized zooids that together handle feeding, floating and jet propulsion — what marine organism is this?
Siphonophore (from Ancient Greek (siphn), meaning "tube" and - (-phros), meaning "bearing") are cnidarian animals of the hydrozoan order Siphonophorae.
Haunted by the Holocaust and the Eichmann trial, this American social psychologist ran his notorious obedience experiments in a Yale basement in 1961. Who was he?
Stanley Milgram (August 15, 1933 - December 20, 1984) was an American social psychologist who conducted controversial experiments on obedience in the 1960s during his professorship at Yale.
A military engineer celebrated as a national hero in Poland, Lithuania, Belarus AND the United States, he fought for American independence before leading an 1794 uprising back home — who was he?

Tadeusz Kościuszko (4 or 12 February 1746 - 15 October 1817) was a Polish military engineer, statesman, and military leader who became a national hero in Poland, the United States, Lithuania, and Belarus.
What culinary herb — the dried aerial parts of plants in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean — is most commonly cultivated in its 'vulgaris' species from Southeast Europe?
Thyme is a culinary herb consisting of the dried aerial parts of some members of the genus Thymus of flowering plants in the mint family Lamiaceae.
Developed by Microsoft as open-source software, this programming language adds optional static typing to JavaScript and transpiles back into it — name the language?
TypeScript (TS) is a high-level programming language that adds static typing with optional type annotations to JavaScript.
One of the oldest leaf vegetables eaten by humans, this fast-growing aquatic plant in the cabbage family shares its peppery bite with relatives like mustard, radish, and wasabi — what plant is it?
Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) is a species of aquatic flowering plant in the cabbage family, Brassicaceae.

This scientific discipline studies the structure, classification, behavior, and distribution of animals both living and extinct, and its name derives from the Greek word for 'animal' — name this field?
Zoology (zoh-, UK also zoo-) is the scientific study of animals.
Regarded as one of Formula One's greatest engineers, his car designs have won 14 Drivers' and 12 Constructors' Championships across three decades?
Adrian Newey: British engineer, aerodynamicist and motorsport executive (born 1958)

This American biologist founded a university institute for sex research in 1947 and gave his name to a scale measuring sexual orientation, after publishing landmark but controversial reports on human sexuality. Who was he?
First identified as a chemical in 1887 and later marketed as the drug Benzedrine, this CNS stimulant is prescribed today for ADHD and narcolepsy — which drug?
This Soviet single-engine biplane, in production from 1947 to 2001, doubles as a crop-duster, water bomber, and paratroop transport thanks to its rugged, adaptable airframe — what is it?
Antonov An-2: Soviet single-engine civilian aircraft.
This order of even-toed hoofed mammals turns out to include whales and dolphins, molecular biology having revealed their close kinship to hippos — what order is it?
Artiodactyla: Order of mammals. Artiodactyla ( AR-tee-oh-DAK-tih-lə; from Ancient Greek ἄρτιος ártios 'even' and δάκτυλος dáktylos 'finger, toe') is an order of placental mammals.

Among the first life forms on Earth and typically just a few micrometres long, these single-celled prokaryotes thrive everywhere from hot springs to radioactive waste and drive the putrefaction stage of decay — what are they?

This steel-gray, brittle alkaline earth metal is found naturally only in combination with other elements, making up gemstones like aquamarine and emerald, and bonds so strongly to oxygen that extracting it is notoriously difficult — which element, atomic number 4?
Beryllium: Chemical element with atomic number 4 (Be)
Conceived for Pan Am as a jet two-and-a-half times the size of the 707, this wide-body, led by designer Joe Sutter, rolled out of the world's largest building in 1968 — which airliner is it?
Boeing 747: American wide-body four-engined jet long-range aircraft.
Often called a 'chest cold,' this inflammation of the airways typically causes a cough lasting around three weeks and is usually caused by a virus?
Bronchitis: Inflammation of the large airways in the lungs.
Originally defined as the heat needed to raise one milliliter of water by one degree Celsius, this unit of energy in nutrition actually refers to a kilocalorie — what is it?

Calorie: Unit of energy used in nutrition. The small calorie or gram calorie is defined as the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one milliliter of water by one degree Celsius (or one kelvin).
Blending science, aesthetics, and technique, this discipline wrestles with projecting a round world onto flat media while deciding what details to keep or cut — what is it called?
Cartography: Study and practice of making maps.
Beyond the resistance-measuring "bridge" that carries his name, this English inventor also gave us the stereoscope, the English concertina, and the Playfair cipher — who was he?
Charles Wheatstone: English physicist and inventor (1802–1875)

Unlike oysters and mussels, which attach to a surface, or scallops, which live near the bottom, this bivalve mollusk instead burrows into sand or mud on the sea floor — what is it, the namesake of a popular chowder?
Clam: Common name for several kinds of bivalve mollusc.

This medium-sized bird of prey ranges across Europe into northwestern China, hunting rodents like voles from a perch, with northern populations migrating as far as South Africa for winter — what bird is this?
Common buzzard: Species of bird of prey. It is a member of the genus Buteo in the family Accipitridae.
Domesticated in Africa and thriving in sandy, low-rainfall soil, this ancient legume is now grown mostly in Nigeria and Niger, which together supply two-thirds of the world's crop — which plant?
Cowpea: Species of plant. The cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.
Son of a bass-baritone and born into a family of engineers, this American built his first car at 19, won four F1 Grands Prix, and took Le Mans in 1967 — who was he?
Dan Gurney: American racing driver, engineer and motorsport executive (1931–2018)
Nicknamed 'dumb cane' because its poisonous sap can temporarily rob you of speech, this shade-tolerant tropical houseplant is native to the New World — which genus?
Dieffenbachia: Genus of plants. Dieffenbachia, commonly known as dumb cane or leopard lily, is a genus of tropical flowering plants in the family Araceae.
This plant genus in the mallow family produces the world's most famously pungent fruit, alongside eight other edible-fruit-bearing species — which genus?
Durio: Genus of plants. Several species produce an edible fruit known as durian, the most common species being Durio zibethinus, with eight others producing edible fruit.
A Swedish scientist and inventor until, at 53, dreams and visions sent him into a spiritual phase, this polymath became best known for his 1758 book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell — who was he?
Emanuel Swedenborg: Swedish scientist, philosopher, and theologian (1688–1772)
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
First described from a skull in 1846 and initially mistaken for a porpoise, this highly social oceanic dolphin gets its common name from a skull resembling that of the orca — which species?
False killer whale: Species of oceanic dolphin in the genus Pseudorca.
Discovered in Dubna in 1999, this superheavy synthetic element (number 114) honors a Russian physicist whose name in Cyrillic explains why its spelling swaps a 'yo' for an 'e' — which element?
Flerovium: Chemical element with atomic number 114 (Fl)
This Canadian physician and author has written five books linking childhood trauma to conditions like ADHD and addiction, though critics question the evidence behind some claims — who is he?

Caused by excess growth hormone before a child's growth plates fuse — usually from a pituitary tumor — this rare disorder produces height at least three standard deviations above average. What condition is it?
Gigantism: Human growth disorder. It is a rare disorder resulting from increased levels of growth hormone before the fusion of the growth plate which usually occurs at some point soon after puberty.
One of the heaviest snakes alive, which non-venomous constrictor prefers shallow, slow-moving South American waters like flooded grasslands and rivers?
An English GP convicted in 2000 of murdering 15 patients, he's reckoned one of history's most prolific serial killers with an estimated 250 victims — who was he?
Harold Shipman: English doctor and serial killer (1946–2004)

This American philosopher co-created an algorithm for the Boolean satisfiability problem and helped prove Hilbert's tenth problem unsolvable — all while reshaping the philosophy of mind and language. Who was he?
Hilary Putnam: American mathematician and philosopher (1926–2016)
Marketed under the brand name Plaquenil, this oral medication treats malaria as well as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, though it can cause retinopathy with long-term use — what drug is it?
Hydroxychloroquine: Antimalarial medication. It is taken by mouth, often in the form of hydroxychloroquine sulfate.
Expressed with symbols like < and >, this relation shows that one quantity is less than or greater than another, rather than equal — what's it called?
Inequality (mathematics): Mathematical relation making a non-equal comparison.

His 1962 book The Calculus of Consent launched a theory of how politicians' and bureaucrats' self-interest shapes their decisions, earning him the 1986 Nobel in economics — which founder of public choice theory is this?
James M. Buchanan: American economist and Nobel Laureate (1919–2013)
This British-American designer ran industrial design at Apple alongside Steve Jobs, then founded the creative collective LoveFrom working with Ferrari and OpenAI — who is he?
This Gram-negative rod bacterium can turn deadly if aspirated into the lungs, producing a telltale bloody, brownish-yellow jelly-like sputum — which pathogen?
Klebsiella pneumoniae: Species of bacterium. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a Gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated, lactose-fermenting, facultative anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium.

Named from the Greek word for 'honey bee' because its flowers attract them, this citrus-scented herb in the mint family has been cultivated since at least the 16th century for tea and aromatic oils — what is it?

Three of this crustacean's five pairs of legs bear claws, with the first pair often dramatically oversized, and its burrow-dwelling relatives include the Norway variety known as langoustine - which creature?
Lobster: Family of clawed marine crustaceans.
With deeply forked tails and iridescent, tiger-like stripes on their backs, these pelagic fish migrate in huge schools to shallow coastal spawning grounds — what are they?
Mackerel: Pelagic fish. Mackerel is a common name applied to a number of different species of pelagic fish, mostly from the family Scombridae.

In 1835 this Scottish polymath and Caroline Herschel became the first female Honorary Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, and she signed first on John Stuart Mill's 1866 petition for women's suffrage — who was she?

Diagnosed when a person has at least three of five red flags -- including abdominal obesity and high blood pressure -- this cluster of conditions raises the risk of heart disease and diabetes in about a quarter of US adults. What is it?
Metabolic syndrome: Cluster of diseases occurring with obesity.
Nicknamed the 'sensitive plant,' this legume's leaves fold inward within seconds of being touched and reopen a few minutes later — what plant is it?
Mimosa pudica: Species of creeping annual plant.
Serving King Roger II in Norman Sicily, this Arab geographer created the Tabula Rogeriana, one of the most advanced world maps of the medieval era — who was he?
Carried harmlessly in the noses of about 10% of adults, this bacterium is the only cause of bacterial meningitis known to occur in epidemics, especially across Africa and Asia — which microbe?
Neisseria meningitidis: Species of bacterium that can cause meningitis.
A subsonic flying wing with a crew of two to three, this nuclear-capable stealth aircraft was built to slip past sophisticated air defenses for the US Air Force — what is it?
Northrop B-2 Spirit: American heavy strategic bomber.

Sitting between tissue and a full body system in life's hierarchy, this general term describes a structural unit built from functional tissue (parenchyma) plus supportive tissue (stroma), as seen in the intestinal wall — what is such a unit called?
Organ (biology): Collection of tissues with similar functions.
This skin sensation includes the classic 'pins and needles' feeling when a limb falls asleep, and can also be triggered by hitting your funny bone — what is it called?
Paresthesia: Dermal sensation with no physical cause.
Created by Larry Wall in 1987 as a Unix scripting tool for report processing, this language's planned sixth version was eventually spun off and renamed Raku — which programming language?
Perl: Interpreted programming language first released in 1987.
This Dutch experimental physicist shared the 1902 Nobel Prize with Hendrik Lorentz for discovering and explaining an effect that now bears his name — who was he?
Covered in sharp keratin quills for defense, this rodent's largest species ranks as the third-biggest living rodent in the world, behind only the capybara and the beaver. What animal is it?
Porcupine: Rodent with a coat of sharp spines.
Nicknamed 'gold cap' and 'golden halo,' this is the world's best-known psilocybin-containing mushroom thanks to its wide distribution and how easily it's cultivated — which species?
Psilocybe cubensis: Species of fungus. It belongs to the fungus family Hymenogastraceae and was previously known as Stropharia cubensis.
Also known as steelhead in its sea-run form, this North American Pacific species shows off a vivid reddish stripe along its flank in breeding males — which fish?
Rainbow trout: Fresh-water species of fish.
Made of a large and small subunit built from RNA and protein, which cellular structure translates messenger RNA into chains of amino acids?
Ribosome: Macromolecular machine that synthesizes proteins in cells.

Built by a Swedish manufacturer, this single-engine fighter was the first mass-produced canard-design aircraft and the first with a digital avionics computer, unsurpassed until the Tornado arrived in 1981 — which jet?
Saab 37 Viggen: 1967 Swedish fighter aircraft family.
Native to cold-temperate Eurasia, this spiny deciduous shrub yields a fruit and oil prized in both cooking and cosmetics — what plant is it?
Sea buckthorn: Species of flowering plant in the family Elaeagnaceae.
Sitting just below carbon in group 14 of the periodic table, this blue-grey, brittle semiconductor is essential to plants and dominates the world's transistors and solar cells — which element is it?
Silicon: Chemical element with atomic number 14 (Si)
Commonly grown as an easy-care houseplant that tolerates low light, this genus of about 60 tropical species is better known by the nickname 'peace lily' — what genus is it?
Spathiphyllum: Genus of plants. Certain species of Spathiphyllum are commonly known as spath or peace lilies.
This throat infection causes fever, red tonsils, and swollen neck glands, and can trigger a sandpaper-textured rash known as scarlet fever — which condition?
Streptococcal pharyngitis: Medical condition. It may be spread directly through touching infected sores.
The lone species in its genus, this African-born leguminous tree gives pods of sweet-tangy pulp used in cuisines worldwide, plus a seed oil and even a dye — what is it?
Tamarind: Leguminous tree bearing edible fruit.
A cousin of caffeine found in trace amounts in tea, coffee, and chocolate, which methylxanthine drug is used to treat asthma and COPD by blocking adenosine receptors?
Theophylline: Drug used to treat respiratory diseases.
